    Where every listing comes from

    No CVE lands on comfypwn.com from a single feed. Each listing is assembled from the public records, exploitation catalogs, vendor advisories, and telemetry below — every source name links to its official site, and every card on the feed links back to the record it came from.

    Last updated: Oct 27 hourly scan — 247 CVEs tracked

    CVE records & scores

    The record itself

    The canonical write-ups: IDs, descriptions, affected products, and the CVSS scores the feed sorts by.

    NVD — National Vulnerability Database ↗

    CVSS scores and the enriched CVE records the listings are built on.

    nvd.nist.gov

    CVE.org / CVE Program ↗

    CVE IDs and the CNA records behind them — the feed that catches CVEs before NVD enrichment lands.

    cve.org

    GitHub Advisory Database ↗

    Advisories and GHSA records, especially for open-source packages and libraries.

    github.com/advisories

    OSV.dev ↗

    Open-source vulnerability data in the OSV schema — affected version ranges across ecosystems.

    osv.dev

    EUVD — European Vulnerability Database ↗

    Supplementary records from ENISA that cross-check and fill gaps in the primary feeds.

    euvd.enisa.europa.eu

    Exploitation status

    Is it being used?

    The catalogs that decide whether a flaw is merely severe or actively dangerous — they drive the In the Wild and CISA KEV tiers.

    CISA KEV — Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog ↗

    Confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, straight from CISA — the listing that moves a CVE into the KEV tier.

    cisa.gov

    VulnCheck KEV ↗

    Earlier exploitation signals — VulnCheck often records exploitation days before the CISA listing lands.

    vulncheck.com/kev

    Vendor advisories

    Fixes, from the source

    Fixes, affected versions, and vendor severity come from the vendor's own advisory — checked directly, not via summaries.

    F5 security advisories (K articles) ↗

    BIG-IP and APM fixes — point releases and engineering hotfixes (EHFs) read straight from the K article's fixes column.

    my.f5.com

    Palo Alto Networks ↗

    PAN-OS and product advisories, including Unit 42 in-the-wild reporting.

    security.paloaltonetworks.com

    Cisco PSIRT ↗

    Cisco security advisories with fixed software releases and workarounds.

    sec.cloudapps.cisco.com

    Fortinet PSIRT ↗

    FortiGuard PSIRT advisories for FortiOS and the rest of the Fortinet line.

    fortiguard.com/psirt

    GitLab ↗

    GitLab security releases — fixed versions for CE/EE, published ahead of the CVE records.

    about.gitlab.com/releases

    Microsoft MSRC ↗

    The Security Update Guide — Microsoft's CVE records, severity, and fix information.

    msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide

    Ivanti ↗

    Ivanti security advisories for Connect Secure, EPMM, and the rest of the edge-device line.

    ivanti.com

    Node.js ↗

    Node.js security releases — runtime flaws and the versions that fix them.

    nodejs.org

    PHP ↗

    PHP release announcements — security fixes shipped in each point release.

    php.net

    Early signals

    Before it's official

    Pre-CVE and pre-confirmation signals. Anything that starts here is labeled an early signal on the feed until a vendor or CERT confirms it.

    Exploit-DB ↗

    Public exploits and proof-of-concepts — a listing here can move a CVE into the Public PoC tier.

    exploit-db.com

    Sploitus ↗

    Exploit search across public sources — catches PoCs that surface outside the usual channels.

    sploitus.com

    Public GitHub PoC / exploit aggregators ↗

    Aggregators that index proof-of-concept code published on GitHub, watched for new weaponized PoCs.

    github.com

    Credible researcher disclosures

    Write-ups and advance disclosures from established security researchers — credited on the listing they feed.

    Vendor advance notices

    Heads-up notices vendors publish before a full advisory or CVE record exists.

    GreyNoise ↗

    Internet-wide scanning and exploitation telemetry — mass-exploitation attempts as they happen.

    greynoise.io

    Shadowserver ↗

    Exploitation telemetry and exposed-device reporting from the Shadowserver Foundation.

    shadowserver.org

    How listings are built

    C:\COMFYPWN> SCAN.EXE — HOURLY, EVERY DAY OF THE WEEK

    Listings come from hourly scans across the sources above. A CVE is tracked when it meets any of these:

    • it scores CVSS 8.0 or higher;
    • it is RCE-class on application security or management / admin interfaces;
    • it grants management / administrative access.

    The score shown is the highest published — vendor or NVD. Every tracked CVE sits in exactly one tier, highest urgency first:

    IN THE WILDCISA KEVPUBLIC POCONES TO WATCHEVERYTHING ELSE

    Early signals are labeled as such until vendor- or CERT-confirmed — a PoC repo or a telemetry hit starts a listing, it doesn't finish one.
